author: Marcus Aurelius
text: A happy lot is this: good inclinations of the soul, good desires, good actions.
original: A happy lot and portion is, good inclinations of the soul, good desires, good actions.
significance: Real good fortune is inward: a well-ordered heart, right desires and good deeds, which no market crash or bad week can take away.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember that everything is only opinion, and all opinion depends on the mind.
original: Remember that all is but opinion, and all opinion depends of the mind.
significance: Much of what upsets you is your judgment about events, not the events themselves, so changing your view can change your day.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To put it in a few words: life is short; we must try to make the most of the present with sound judgment and justice.
original: To comprehend all in a few words, our life is short; we must endeavour to gain the present time with best discretion and justice.
significance: Life is short, so spend the hour in front of you wisely and fairly rather than waiting for a better moment that may not come.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: This is what a happy life consists of: to know thoroughly the true nature of everything, what its substance is and what its form; and with all your heart and soul always to do what is just and to speak the truth.
original: Herein doth consist happiness of life, for a man to know thoroughly the true nature of everything; what is the matter, and what is the form of it: with all his heart and soul, ever to do that which is just, and to speak the truth.
significance: A good life comes from seeing things as they truly are, then wholeheartedly doing what is right and telling the truth.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Always keep your purpose and resolve free from all compulsion and necessity.
original: Ever maintain thine own purpose and resolution free from all compulsion and necessity.
significance: Hold to your chosen purpose freely; pressure from others or circumstances should not decide what kind of person you are.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Every person's happiness depends on themselves, yet look: your life is almost over, and while you show yourself no respect, you make your happiness depend on the minds and opinions of other people.
original: Every man's happiness depends from himself, but behold thy life is almost at an end, whiles affording thyself no respect, thou dost make thy happiness to consist in the souls, and conceits of other men.
significance: Making your happiness depend on what others think hands them control of your life; your worth rests on your own conduct.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whenever you choose, you can withdraw into yourself and be at rest, free from all your business.
original: At what time soever thou wilt, it is in thy power to retire into thyself, and to be at rest, and free from all businesses.
significance: Peace is always available within; even in a busy day you can step back into your own mind and find calm.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To live happily is a power within the soul, when it stays indifferent toward things that are by nature indifferent.
original: To live happily is an inward power of the soul, when she is affected with indifferency, towards those things that are by their nature indifferent.
significance: Contentment comes from not being disturbed by things that are neither good nor bad in themselves, like money, status or comfort.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let this be your only joy and your only comfort: to pass without pause from one kind, sociable act to the next, always keeping God in mind.
original: Let this be thy only joy, and thy only comfort, from one sociable kind action without intermission to pass unto another, God being ever in thy mind.
significance: Joy can be found in moving from one act of kindness to the next while keeping God in mind throughout the day.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Death hangs over you: while you are still alive, while you still can, be good.
original: Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good.
significance: Death is near for everyone, so the time to be good is today, while you still can, not someday later.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Shrink your whole life down to the measure of one single action.
original: Contract thy whole life to the measure and proportion of one single action.
significance: Treat your whole life with the focus of a single task: do each thing fully and well, one action at a time.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Wherever you happen to live, you can live well and happily there.
original: Wheresoever thou mayest live, there it is in thy power to live well and happy.
significance: Circumstances do not decide whether you can live well; wherever you are placed, a good life is still within reach.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Kind actions and a holy disposition are the only fruit of this earthly life.
original: Charitable actions, and a holy disposition, is the only fruit of this earthly life.
significance: The lasting fruit of a life is kindness toward others and a reverent heart, not wealth or reputation.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Give yourself time to learn something good, and stop roaming and wandering back and forth.
original: Give thyself leisure to learn some good thing, and cease roving and wandering to and fro.
significance: Make time to learn something worthwhile, and stop drifting between distractions that leave you no wiser.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: So keep yourself truly simple, good, sincere, serious, free from all showing off, a lover of justice, devout, kind, tender-hearted, and strong and ready to undertake anything that befits you.
original: Keep thyself therefore, truly simple, good, sincere, grave, free from all ostentation, a lover of that which is just, religious, kind, tender-hearted, strong and vigorous to undergo anything that becomes thee.
significance: A good person is simple, sincere and unpretentious, loves justice, is gentle, and is strong enough to carry hard duties.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: So take the trouble to learn what your nature requires, and let nothing else distract you.
original: Take pains therefore to know what it is that thy nature requireth, and let nothing else distract thee.
significance: Work out what your nature and calling truly require of you, and refuse to be pulled off course by everything else.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To righteousness, in speaking the truth freely, and without ambiguity; and in doing all things justly and discreetly.
significance: Justice means speaking the truth plainly and without spin, and acting fairly and wisely in every matter.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let no one be able to say truthfully of you that you are not simple, sincere and open, or not good.
original: Let it not be in any man's power, to say truly of thee, that thou art not truly simple, or sincere and open, or not good.
significance: Live so that no one could honestly accuse you of being insincere, devious or unkind; let your character answer for you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: An angry face is completely against nature, and it is often the very face of those who are about to die.
original: An angry countenance is much against nature, and it is oftentimes the proper countenance of them that are at the point of death.
significance: Anger distorts the face and the self; a scowl is unnatural, a sign of something going wrong inside rather than strength.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Everything you hope to reach in the future you can enjoy and possess right now, if you do not deny yourself your own happiness.
original: Whatsoever thou doest hereafter aspire unto, thou mayest even now enjoy and possess, if thou doest not envy thyself thine own happiness.
significance: The peace and goodness you hope to reach someday can be yours now, if you stop postponing them and choose them today.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Death is a cessation from the impression of the senses, the tyranny of the passions, the errors of the mind, and the servitude of the body.
significance: Marcus pictures death as release from the pull of the senses, the tyranny of passions and the errors of the mind.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Stop arguing and talking about what the marks of a good person are, and actually be one.
original: Make it not any longer a matter of dispute or discourse, what are the signs and proprieties of a good man, but really and actually to be such.
significance: Stop debating what makes a good person and simply be one; character shows in what you do, not what you discuss.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In the morning, when you find yourself unwilling to get up, tell yourself at once: I am getting up to do a human being's work.
original: In the morning when thou findest thyself unwilling to rise, consider with thyself presently, it is to go about a man's work that I am stirred up.
significance: When duty is hard to face in the morning, remember you are getting up to do the work you were made to do.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If anyone corrects me and shows me clearly that I am wrong in any opinion or action of mine, I will gladly change my mind.
original: If anybody shall reprove me, and shall make it apparent unto me, that in any either opinion or action of mine I do err, I will most gladly retract.
significance: A wise person welcomes correction; being shown your error is a gift, and changing your mind is a strength.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let us do our best to persuade them; but if reason and justice lead you to it, do it anyway, however much they oppose it.
original: Let us do our best endeavours to persuade them; but however, if reason and justice lead thee to it, do it, though they be never so much against it.
significance: Try to persuade people, but if reason and justice demand an action, do the right thing even when others object.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What use is suspicion at all? Why should mistrustful thoughts and suspicion about the future trouble your mind at all?
original: What use is there of suspicion at all? or, why should thoughts of mistrust, and suspicion concerning that which is future, trouble thy mind at all?
significance: Suspicion and worry about what might happen only disturb the mind; they rarely prevent anything and often poison trust.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When someone's wrongdoing offends you, immediately turn to yourself and consider how you are guilty of the same kind of thing.
original: When thou art offended with any man's transgression, presently reflect upon thyself; and consider what thou thyself art guilty of in the same kind.
significance: When someone's fault annoys you, first ask where you fail in the same way; it softens judgment and makes you humbler.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Make it a habit, whenever you see anyone do anything, to ask yourself at once (if possible): What is this person's aim in doing this?
original: Use thyself; as often, as thou seest any man do anything, presently (if it be possible) to say unto thyself, What is this man's end in this his action?
significance: Train yourself to ask what a person is aiming at; understanding motives helps you respond wisely instead of reacting.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The time of a man's life is as a point; the substance of it ever flowing, the sense obscure; and the whole composition of the body tending to corruption.
significance: Life is brief and fleeting, so do not cling to it or waste it; use the short span you have for what matters.

author: Epictetus
text: Within our power are opinion, aim, desire, aversion, and, in one word, whatever affairs are our own.
significance: Only your judgments, aims, desires and choices are truly yours; focus your energy there rather than on what you cannot control.

author: Epictetus
text: When you set about any action, remind yourself of what nature the action is.
significance: Before you start something, picture what it will really involve, so that its normal frustrations do not knock you off balance.

author: Epictetus
text: If it be his pleasure that you should enact a poor man, or a cripple, or a ruler, or a private citizen, see that you act it well.
significance: Whatever role God gives you, rich or poor, leader or private citizen, your task is to play it well, not to choose it.

author: Epictetus
text: You must cultivate either your own reason or else externals; apply yourself either to things within or without you—that is, be either a philosopher or one of the mob.
significance: You must decide what you are cultivating: either your inner character or outward things; you cannot fully serve both.

author: Epictetus
text: In our power are our thinking, our intentions, our desires, our decisions.
significance: Your thoughts, intentions, desires and decisions are the part of life you truly govern, so guard them carefully.

author: Epictetus
text: In company, avoid a frequent and excessive mention of your own actions and dangers.
significance: Avoid talking much about your own exploits; constant self-reference wearies others and feeds pride.

author: Epictetus
text: If you wish your children and your wife and your friends to live forever, you are foolish, for you wish things to be in your power which are not so, and what belongs to others to be your own.
significance: Loving family and friends is right, but demanding they never die is demanding control you do not have; hold them gratefully.

author: Epictetus
text: When, therefore, anyone provokes you, be assured that it is your own opinion which provokes you.
significance: Others cannot make you angry without your consent; it is your own judgment that turns an insult into an injury.

author: Epictetus
text: Never proclaim yourself a philosopher, nor make much talk among the ignorant about your principles, but show them by actions.
significance: Do not announce your principles or lecture people about them; let your conduct quietly show what you believe.

author: Epictetus
text: If you encounter a handsome person, you will find continence the faculty needed; if pain, then fortitude; if reviling, then patience.
significance: Every trial is a call for a specific virtue: temptation calls for self-control, pain for courage, insults for patience.

author: Epictetus
text: How long, then, will you delay to demand of yourself the noblest improvements, and in no instance to transgress the judgments of reason?
significance: Stop putting off the effort to become better; there is no reason to wait to live by what you know is right.

author: Epictetus
text: If you ever happen to turn your attention to externals, for the pleasure of anyone, be assured that you have ruined your scheme of life.
significance: The moment you shape your life around pleasing others, you have abandoned your own course and principles.

author: Epictetus
text: Let death and exile, and all other things which appear terrible, be daily before your eyes, but death chiefly; and you will never entertain an abject thought, nor too eagerly covet anything.
significance: Keeping death in view daily cures petty thoughts and greedy cravings, and helps you live with seriousness and freedom.

author: Epictetus
text: If, then, you shun only those undesirable things which you can control, you will never incur anything which you shun; but if you shun sickness, or death, or poverty, you will run the risk of wretchedness.
significance: If you only fear the wrongs you can avoid, like your own bad choices, you will not be crushed by what lies beyond you.

author: Epictetus
text: Great is the combat, divine is the work; it is for kingship, for freedom, for happiness, for freedom from perturbation.
significance: The struggle for self-mastery is the noblest work there is, because it wins freedom, happiness and a calm mind.

author: Epictetus
text: When you are going to take in hand any act remind yourself what kind of an act it is.
significance: Before acting, consider what kind of act it is, so you can meet its difficulties with a clear head.

author: Epictetus
text: Every habit and faculty is maintained and increased by the corresponding actions: the habit of walking by walking, the habit of running by running.
significance: Habits grow by practice, good or bad; whatever you repeatedly do, you become better at and more inclined toward.

author: Epictetus
text: Have you taken pains to learn what is a good man and what is a bad man, and how a man becomes one or the other?
significance: Before you can become a good person you need to understand what goodness is and how character is formed or lost.

author: Epictetus
text: Each man is improved and preserved by corresponding acts, the carpenter by acts of carpentry, the grammarian by acts of grammar.
significance: Skill and character grow by doing: a carpenter improves by building, and a person grows in virtue by acting virtuously.

author: Epictetus
text: My man, first of all consider what kind of thing it is; and then examine your own nature, if you are able to sustain the character.
significance: Before taking on a role, honestly weigh both what it demands and whether you have the strength to carry it.

author: Epictetus
text: If a man is unhappy, remember that his unhappiness is his own fault; for God has made all men to be happy, to be free from perturbations.
significance: Epictetus taught that unhappiness flows from our own false judgments, since God made people capable of peace and contentment.

author: Epictetus
text: Does it seem to you so small and worthless a thing to be good and happy?
significance: Being good and at peace is not a small goal; it is the most worthwhile achievement of a life, worth every effort.

author: Epictetus
text: If labor (pain) be presented to you, you will find that it is endurance.
significance: Hardship is not only something to avoid; it is a chance to practise endurance, the virtue made for that moment.

author: Epictetus
text: Keep by every means what is your own; do not desire what belongs to others.
significance: Guard what is truly yours, your character and choices, and do not covet what belongs to someone else.

author: Epictetus
text: Do you seek a reward for a good man greater than doing what is good and just?
significance: Doing good is its own reward; needing praise or payment for being just misses the point of goodness.

author: Epictetus
text: What then, since I am naturally dull, shall I, for this reason, take no pains?
significance: Lacking natural talent is no excuse to stop trying; effort still improves you, whatever your starting point.

author: Epictetus
text: Take care then when you observe a man honored before others or possessed of great power or highly esteemed for any reason, not to suppose him happy, and be not carried away by the appearance.
significance: Do not envy people with power, status or honour; outward success says nothing about whether their life is truly good.

author: Epictetus
text: May it never be my lot to have a wise fool for my friend; nothing is more untractable.
significance: A clever person without humility is the hardest friend to have, because they will not be taught or corrected.

author: Epictetus
text: Whomsoever then it is in the power of another to hinder and compel, declare that he is not free.
significance: Anyone who can be controlled by another through what he wants or fears is not truly free.

author: Epictetus
text: In walking about, as you take care not to step on a nail, or to sprain your foot, so take care not to damage your own ruling faculty; and if we observe this rule in every act, we shall undertake this act with more security.
significance: As you watch your step to avoid injury, guard your mind and judgment in every action, since that hurt is worse.

author: Epictetus
text: Come and you will know what poverty is when it has found one who can act well the part of a poor man.
significance: Poverty is no disgrace when borne well; a good person shows how even a humble lot can be lived with dignity.

author: Epictetus
text: In every act observe the things which come first, and those which follow it; and so proceed to the act.
significance: Before acting, think through what comes first and what will follow, so you are not surprised by consequences.

author: Epictetus
text: Man, consider first what the matter is (which you propose to do), then your own nature also, what it is able to bear.
significance: Before starting something, examine both the task and your own capacity to carry it through.

author: Epictetus
text: If then we shall not also put in practice right opinions, we shall be nothing more than the expositors of the opinions of others.
significance: Knowing good principles is not enough; unless you practise them, you are only repeating other people's ideas.

author: Epictetus
text: Only consider at what price you sell your own will: if for no other reason, at least for this, that you sell it not for a small sum.
significance: Your will and integrity have a price only if you set one; never sell them, least of all for something cheap.

author: Epictetus
text: Be willing at length to be approved by yourself, be willing to appear beautiful to God, desire to be in purity with your own pure self and with God.
significance: Seek the approval of your own conscience and of God, rather than the applause of the crowd.

author: Seneca
text: Cast away everything of that sort, if you are wise; nay, rather that you may be wise; strive toward a sound mind at top speed and with your whole strength.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Let go of empty pursuits and pursue a sound mind with all your energy; wisdom is worth your full strength.

author: Seneca
text: Counting even yesterday, all past time is lost time; the very day which we are now spending is shared between ourselves and death.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Time already gone is lost to us, and even today is slipping toward death, so use each day with care.

author: Seneca
text: What they wish to have heaped upon you are not really good things; there is only one good, the cause and the support of a happy life,—trust in oneself.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: The things others wish on you, wealth and honours, are not true goods; a happy life rests on a steady trust in what is right.

author: Seneca
text: Most men ebb and flow in wretchedness between the fear of death and the hardships of life; they are unwilling to live, and yet they do not know how to die.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Many people are stuck between fear of dying and dread of living; learning to face death frees you to live well.

author: Seneca
text: If you wish to have leisure for your mind, either be a poor man, or resemble a poor man.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Wanting little frees your mind; whether or not you are poor, living simply leaves room for what matters.

author: Seneca
text: When friendship is settled, you must trust; before friendship is formed, you must pass judgment.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Take time deciding whom to trust as a friend; once you have decided, trust them fully and without suspicion.

author: Seneca
text: Make yourself happy through your own efforts; you can do this, if once you comprehend that whatever is blended with virtue is good, and that whatever is joined to vice is bad.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Happiness comes from your own efforts at goodness, once you see that virtue is the real good and vice the real harm.

author: Seneca
text: The things which we actually need are free for all, or else cheap; nature craves only bread and water.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: What we truly need is cheap and available; most of what we chase is extra that nature never asked for.

author: Seneca
text: Why, indeed, is it necessary to summon trouble,—which must be endured soon enough when it has once arrived,—or to anticipate trouble and ruin the present through fear of the future?
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Do not borrow trouble; worrying about future misfortune spoils the present and adds suffering that may never come.

author: Seneca
text: Riches have shut off many a man from the attainment of wisdom; poverty is unburdened and free from care.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Wealth can crowd out wisdom by filling life with cares; having less can leave the mind freer for what matters.

author: Seneca
text: Judgment varies from day to day, and changes to the opposite, making many a man pass his life in a kind of game.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Without steady principles, people change their minds day by day and treat life like a game with no settled aim.

author: Seneca
text: The beginning is in our own power; fortune decides the issue, but I do not allow her to pass sentence upon myself.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: You control how you begin and how you act; outcomes are up to fortune, but they cannot decide your worth.

author: Seneca
text: You must persevere, must develop new strength by continuous study, until that which is only a good inclination becomes a good settled purpose.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Good intentions must be strengthened by steady practice until they become settled character.

author: Seneca
text: Without philosophy the mind is sickly, and the body, too, though it may be very powerful, is strong only as that of a madman or a lunatic is strong.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: A strong body without a wise mind is like the strength of a madman; inner health matters more than outward strength.

author: Seneca
text: We reach death at that moment, but we have been a long time on the way.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Death is not a single moment far ahead; we have been moving toward it every day, so live each day well.

author: Seneca
text: Ponder for a long time whether you shall admit a given person to your friendship; but when you have decided to admit him, welcome him with all your heart and soul.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Think carefully before accepting someone as a close friend, but once you do, welcome them wholeheartedly.

author: Seneca
text: Do you, however, always think on death in order that you may never fear it.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Thinking about death regularly takes away its terror and helps you live without fear.

author: Seneca
text: Philosophy itself, however, should be practised with calmness and moderation.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Even the pursuit of wisdom should be calm and moderate, not showy, extreme or harsh.

author: Seneca
text: Philosophy is good advice; and no one can give advice at the top of his lungs.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Good advice is given quietly and patiently; shouting at people rarely helps them see what is right.

author: Seneca
text: No good thing renders its possessor happy, unless his mind is reconciled to the possibility of loss; nothing, however, is lost with less discomfort than that which, when lost, cannot be missed.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Hold good things loosely; if you are prepared to lose them, you can enjoy them without fear.

author: Seneca
text: Of this one thing make sure against your dying day,—let your faults die before you die.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Before you die, aim to see your faults die first; make growth in character the work of your life.

author: Seneca
text: Accordingly, let your thoughts, your efforts, your desires, help to make you content with your own self and with the goods that spring from yourself; and commit all your other prayers to God’s keeping!
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Seek contentment in your own character, and trust God with everything else you might pray for.

author: Seneca
text: Remember, however, before all else, to strip things of all that disturbs and confuses, and to see what each is at bottom; you will then comprehend that they contain nothing fearful except the actual fear.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Strip a situation of its drama and look at what it really is; often the only frightening thing is the fear itself.

author: Seneca
text: Natural desires are limited; but those which spring from false opinion can have no stopping-point.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Natural needs are easily met, but desires based on false opinion never end, so learn to want what you need.

author: Seneca
text: When a person spends all his time in foreign travel, he ends by having many acquaintances, but no friends.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Constant restlessness leaves you with many acquaintances but no deep friendships; depth needs time in one place.

author: Seneca
text: Hold fast to it and establish it firmly, in order that what is now impulse may become a habit of the mind.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Strengthen good resolutions until a passing impulse becomes a settled habit of the mind.

author: Seneca
text: Philosophy calls for plain living, but not for penance; and we may perfectly well be plain and neat at the same time.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Simple living does not mean harsh self-punishment; you can be plain and modest while still being neat and decent.

author: Seneca
text: You must be not only present in the body, but watchful in mind, if you would avail yourself of the fleeting opportunity.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Opportunities pass quickly; you must be mentally alert and engaged, not just physically present, to take them.

author: Seneca
text: The primary indication, to my thinking, of a well-ordered mind is a man’s ability to remain in one place and linger in his own company.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: A settled mind can stay in one place and enjoy its own company, without constant need for change or distraction.

author: Seneca
text: You must linger among a limited number of master-thinkers, and digest their works, if you would derive ideas which shall win firm hold in your mind.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Go deep with a few great teachers rather than skimming many; ideas take root through careful, repeated study.

author: Seneca
text: Choose a master whose life, conversation, and soul-expressing face have satisfied you; picture him always to yourself as your protector or your pattern.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Pick a role model whose life and character you admire, and keep them in mind as both protector and pattern.

author: Seneca
text: Just as the same chain fastens the prisoner and the soldier who guards him, so hope and fear, dissimilar as they are, keep step together; fear follows hope.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Hope and fear are chained together: craving an uncertain future also makes you anxious about it.

author: Seneca
text: I remember one day you were handling the well-known commonplace,—that we do not suddenly fall on death, but advance towards it by slight degrees; we die every day.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: We die little by little each day, so every day is part of life's limited supply and should be used well.

author: Seneca
text: Examine yourself; scrutinize and observe yourself in divers ways; but mark, before all else, whether it is in philosophy or merely in life itself that you have made progress.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Check whether you have grown in how you actually live, not just in what you know or can say.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All men are made one for another: either then teach them better, or bear with them.
significance: People are made to live together, so when others fall short, the choice is to teach them patiently or to bear with them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Either teach them better if you can, or if you cannot, remember that gentleness and goodness were given to you for exactly this: to bear with them patiently.
original: Either teach them better if it be in thy power; or if it be not, remember that for this use, to bear with them patiently, was mildness and goodness granted unto thee.
significance: When you cannot correct someone, gentleness is exactly what patience is for; difficult people are the reason kindness exists.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: There is only one thing in this world worth our while and worth valuing highly: to live with truth and justice, gently and lovingly, among false and unjust people.
original: One thing there is, and that only, which is worth our while in this world, and ought by us much to be esteemed; and that is, according to truth and righteousness, meekly and lovingly to converse with false, and unrighteous men.
significance: The real test of character is staying truthful, fair and gentle with people who are dishonest or unjust toward you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The ambitious person thinks their happiness lies in other people's actions, praise and applause; the pleasure-seeker in their own sensations; but the wise person in their own actions.
original: The ambitious supposeth another man's act, praise and applause, to be his own happiness; the voluptuous his own sense and feeling; but he that is wise, his own action.
significance: The ambitious live for applause and the pleasure-seeker for sensations, but a wise person finds satisfaction in doing right.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whenever someone wrongs another, immediately ask yourself what they believed was good and what was evil when they did it.
original: Whensoever any man doth trespass against other, presently consider with thyself what it was that he did suppose to be good, what to be evil, when he did trespass.
significance: When someone wrongs you, ask what they believed was good or bad; understanding their reasoning turns anger into understanding.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The one who praises and the one who is praised, the one who remembers and the one who is remembered, will all soon be dust and ashes.
original: Both he that praiseth, and he that is praised; he that remembers, and he that is remembered, will soon be dust and ashes.
significance: Praise and reputation are short-lived because everyone involved soon dies, so they are poor things to build a life on.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Stick to the first plain, bare impressions of things as they present themselves to you, and add nothing to them.
original: Keep thyself to the first bare and naked apprehensions of things, as they present themselves unto thee, and add not unto them.
significance: See events as they plainly are and do not pile on stories, fears or insults that you add yourself; that is where distress grows.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Shape yourself, through constant effort, into true freedom with kindness, true simplicity and modesty.
original: Beget thyself by continual pains and endeavours to true liberty with charity, and true simplicity and modesty.
significance: Freedom, love, simplicity and humility are not instant gifts; they are formed in you through steady, daily effort.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: You must not treat death with scorn, but meet it as someone content with it, as one of the things nature has appointed.
original: Thou must not in matter of death carry thyself scornfully, but as one that is well pleased with it, as being one of those things that nature hath appointed.
significance: Face death neither with contempt nor dread, but calmly accept it as part of the order of things you were given.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The effect of true philosophy is, unaffected simplicity and modesty.
significance: Real wisdom does not make you impressive or showy; it makes you simpler, humbler and more genuine.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatever happens to you was appointed for you from all time.
original: Whatsoever it be that happens unto thee, it is that which from all time was appointed unto thee.
significance: What happens to you is not random; accepting your lot as appointed helps you meet each day with trust instead of resentment.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What, then, is the wisest thing that can be said or done in this present situation?
original: What then is it that may upon this present occasion according to best reason and discretion, either be said or done?
significance: In any situation, the useful question is not why this happened, but what is the wisest thing to say or do right now.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: A branch is cut off by something else, but a person who hates and turns away cuts himself off from his neighbour, not realising that he is also cutting himself off from the whole body of society.
original: A branch is cut off by another, but he that hates and is averse, cuts himself off from his neighbour, and knows not that at the same time he divides himself from the whole body, or corporation.
significance: Hatred is self-inflicted exile: whoever cuts himself off from a neighbour also cuts himself off from the community he belongs to.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How fortunate is the power given to us: we need do nothing except what God would approve, and we can contentedly accept whatever God sends us.
original: How happy is man in this his power that hath been granted unto him: that he needs not do anything but what God shall approve, and that he may embrace contentedly, whatsoever God doth send unto him?
significance: We are free to do only what God would approve and to accept contentedly what He sends; that freedom is a great gift.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: So go your way well pleased and content, for so is the One who dismisses you.
original: Go thy ways then well pleased and contented: for so is He that dismisseth thee.
significance: When your time ends, depart with peace and gratitude, for the One who sends you away does so with goodwill.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As your habitual thoughts are, so your mind will become in time.
original: Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy mind be in time.
significance: Your habitual thoughts shape who you become, so what you dwell on each day is slowly forming your character.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How have you behaved so far toward the gods? Toward your parents? Your brothers and sisters? Your wife? Your children? Your teachers? Those who raised you? Your friends? Your household? Your servants?
original: How hast thou carried thyself hitherto towards the Gods? towards thy parents? towards thy brethren? towards thy wife? towards thy children? towards thy masters? thy foster-fathers? thy friends? thy domestics? thy servants?
significance: A searching self-examination: character is measured by how you have treated God, family, teachers, friends and those who serve you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember too how many things you have already been through and how much you have been able to endure, so that the story of your life is now complete and your task fulfilled.
original: Remember withal through how many things thou hast already passed, and how many thou hast been able to endure; so that now the legend of thy life is full, and thy charge is accomplished.
significance: Recall how much you have already come through; past endurance is evidence that you can meet what comes next.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whenever hard circumstances force you to be somewhat troubled and upset, return to yourself as quickly as you can, and do not stay out of tune longer than you must.
original: Whensoever by some present hard occurrences thou art constrained to be in some sort troubled and vexed, return unto thyself as soon as may be, and be not out of tune longer than thou must needs.
significance: Everyone gets rattled sometimes; the skill is to recover your composure quickly instead of staying upset longer than needed.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Stop troubling yourself from now on; bring yourself back to perfect simplicity.
original: Trouble not thyself any more henceforth, reduce thyself unto perfect simplicity.
significance: Much anxiety comes from complicating life; returning to simple duties and simple aims brings quiet back to the mind.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Some people, when they have done someone a favour, are quick to put it on that person's account and expect something in return.
original: Such there be, who when they have done a good turn to any, are ready to set them on the score for it, and to require retaliation.
significance: Some people keep score of every favour and expect repayment; real kindness is given freely without keeping accounts.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatever you pursue, whatever you plan, do and plan it all as someone who, for all you know, may leave this life at this very moment.
original: Whatsoever thou dost affect, whatsoever thou dost project, so do, and so project all, as one who, for aught thou knowest, may at this very present depart out of this life.
significance: Plan and act as someone who could die today; that perspective strips away pettiness and keeps you focused on what matters.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Do not spend the rest of your days thinking and fantasising about other people, unless it serves some common good, when it keeps you from some better work.
original: Spend not the remnant of thy days in thoughts and fancies concerning other men, when it is not in relation to some common good, when by it thou art hindered from some other better work.
significance: Do not waste your limited days speculating about other people's business when it serves no good and keeps you from your own work.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The end and object of a rational constitution is, to do nothing rashly, to be kindly affected towards men, and in all things willingly to submit unto the gods.
significance: A well-ordered mind acts without rashness, wishes others well, and willingly accepts the providence that governs all things.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged.
significance: Much of the hurt we feel comes from our judgment that we have been wronged; drop that judgment and the sting fades.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Certainly there is nothing better, than for a man to confine himself to necessary actions; to such and so many only, as reason in a creature that knows itself born for society, will command and enjoin.
significance: Focus on what truly needs doing for yourself and others; cutting the unnecessary leaves time and calm for the essential.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How easy it is to push away every disturbing, intruding thought, and at once be in perfect rest and calm!
original: How easy a thing is it for a man to put off from him all turbulent adventitious imaginations, and presently to be in perfect rest and tranquillity!
significance: Disturbing thoughts are not fixed; you can set aside the worries your mind invents and return to calm sooner than you think.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Early in the morning, tell yourself: Today I will have to deal with a meddling, nosy person, an ungrateful one, an abusive one, a cunning, false or envious one, an unsociable, uncharitable one.
original: Betimes in the morning say to thyself, This day I shalt have to do with an idle curious man, with an unthankful man, a railer, a crafty, false, or an envious man; an unsociable uncharitable man.
significance: Expect to meet difficult people each day; preparing in advance helps you respond with patience instead of surprise or anger.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: From my grandfather Verus I learned to be gentle and meek, and to hold back from all anger and passion.
original: Of my grandfather Verus I have learned to be gentle and meek, and to refrain from all anger and passion.
significance: Marcus credited his grandfather with teaching him gentleness and self-control; the character of elders shapes the next generation.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: From my mother I learned to be devout and generous; to avoid not only doing evil but even intending it; to be content with a simple diet; and to shun the kind of excess that comes with great wealth.
original: Of my mother I have learned to be religious, and bountiful; and to forbear, not only to do, but to intend any evil; to content myself with a spare diet, and to fly all such excess as is incidental to great wealth.
significance: A mother's example taught Marcus piety, generosity, purity of intention and simple living, even amid great wealth.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatever pain you are in, let this come to mind at once: it is nothing to be ashamed of, and it cannot make your understanding, which governs everything, any worse.
original: What pain soever thou art in, let this presently come to thy mind, that it is not a thing whereof thou needest to be ashamed, neither is it a thing whereby thy understanding, that hath the government of all, can be made worse.
significance: Pain is not shameful and cannot corrupt your mind or character; you can suffer and still remain fully yourself.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: You must constantly think about what kind of people they are, and what state their minds and understanding are in, whose good opinion and praise you want.
original: Thou must continually ponder and consider with thyself, what manner of men they be, and for their minds and understandings what is their present estate, whose good word and testimony thou dost desire.
significance: Before craving someone's approval, consider what kind of people they are; praise is only worth as much as the judgment behind it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If it is not right, do not do it. If it is not true, do not say it.
original: If it be not fitting, do it not. If it be not true, speak it not.
significance: A simple rule for each day: if an action is not right, do not do it; if a statement is not true, do not say it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That which is not good for the bee-hive, cannot be good for the bee.
significance: What harms the community cannot truly benefit the individual; your good is bound up with the good of those around you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Do not let the future trouble you. For if it must come, you will meet it, whenever that is, with the same reason that makes everything present bearable and acceptable to you.
original: Let not things future trouble thee. For if necessity so require that they come to pass, thou shalt (whensoever that is) be provided for them with the same reason, by which whatsoever is now present, is made both tolerable and acceptable unto thee.
significance: Do not dread the future; the same judgment and strength that carry you through today will be there when tomorrow comes.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Do not imagine future things as if they were already here, but of the things you have now, pick out the ones that benefit you most and think carefully how much you would long for them if you did not have them.
original: Fancy not to thyself things future, as though they were present but of those that are present, take some aside, that thou takest most benefit of, and consider of them particularly, how wonderfully thou wouldst want them, if they were not present.
significance: Rather than daydreaming about what you lack, consider the good things you have now and how much you would miss them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If my present judgment of things is right, my present action is loving, and my present attitude is to welcome whatever comes from God, that is enough.
original: If my present apprehension of the object be right, and my present action charitable, and this, towards whatsoever doth proceed from God, be my present disposition, to be well pleased with it, it sufficeth.
significance: It is enough to see the present truly, act lovingly in it, and accept contentedly what God sends; nothing more is required.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Do not be lazy and careless, or loose and reckless in your actions; do not be quarrelsome and difficult in conversation; and do not let your thoughts and imaginings roam and wander.
original: Not to be slack and negligent; or loose, and wanton in thy actions; nor contentious, and troublesome in thy conversation; nor to rove and wander in thy fancies and imaginations.
significance: A compact rule for daily conduct: be diligent in work, disciplined in action, peaceable in speech and focused in thought.

author: Epictetus
text: Where it is practically necessary for you to pursue or avoid anything, do even this with discretion and gentleness and moderation.
significance: Even when you must strive for something or steer clear of it, do it calmly and with restraint rather than with grasping or panic.

author: Epictetus
text: When, therefore, we are hindered or disturbed, or grieved, let us never impute it to others, but to ourselves—that is, to our own views.
significance: When upset, look first at your own judgments rather than blaming others; that is the part you can actually change.

author: Epictetus
text: Demand not that events should happen as you wish; but wish them to happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.
significance: Peace comes from accepting what actually happens instead of insisting that life follow your plans.

author: Epictetus
text: Sickness is an impediment to the body, but not to the will unless itself pleases.
significance: Illness can limit what your body does, but it cannot stop you from choosing to act well and keep a good spirit.

author: Epictetus
text: Upon every accident, remember to turn toward yourself and inquire what faculty you have for its use.
significance: Every setback calls for an inner resource such as patience, courage or self-control; ask which one this moment requires.

author: Epictetus
text: If you would improve, be content to be thought foolish and dull with regard to externals.
significance: Growth sometimes means caring less about status and appearances, even if others think you odd for it.

author: Epictetus
text: Do not desire to be thought to know anything; and though you should appear to others to be somebody, distrust yourself.
significance: Do not chase a reputation for knowledge, and when others admire you, stay humble and keep examining yourself.

author: Epictetus
text: A man’s master is he who is able to confer or remove whatever that man seeks or shuns.
significance: Whoever controls what you crave or fear effectively controls you; wanting less outward things makes you freer.

author: Epictetus
text: Whoever then would be free, let him wish nothing, let him decline nothing, which depends on others; else he must necessarily be a slave.
significance: If your peace depends on what others give or withhold, you are not free; anchor your desires in what is yours to choose.

author: Epictetus
text: Remember that you are an actor in a drama of such sort as the Author chooses—if short, then in a short one; if long, then in a long one.
significance: You do not write the length or plot of your life; your part is to play the role given to you faithfully and well.

author: Epictetus
text: When, therefore, it is our duty to share the danger of a friend or of our country, we ought not to consult the oracle as to whether we shall share it with them or not.
significance: When duty is clear, such as standing by a friend in danger, there is nothing to deliberate; simply do what is right.

author: Epictetus
text: Be mostly silent, or speak merely what is needful, and in few words.
significance: Speak less and say what is needed; fewer words usually carry more weight and cause fewer regrets.

author: Epictetus
text: Provide things relating to the body no further than absolute need requires, as meat, drink, clothing, house, retinue.
significance: Meet your physical needs simply; spending beyond real need on food, clothes and home adds burdens, not happiness.

author: Epictetus
text: If you are dazzled by the semblance of any promised pleasure, guard yourself against being bewildered by it; but let the affair wait your leisure, and procure yourself some delay.
significance: When temptation dazzles you, do not act at once; give yourself time, and the pull usually weakens as reason returns.

author: Epictetus
text: If you have assumed any character beyond your strength, you have both demeaned yourself ill in that and quitted one which you might have supported.
significance: Taking on a role you cannot carry means failing at it and neglecting the role you could have filled well.

author: Epictetus
text: When any person does ill by you, or speaks ill of you, remember that he acts or speaks from an impression that it is right for him to do so.
significance: People who wrong you usually think they are in the right; remembering this makes it easier to respond without bitterness.

author: Epictetus
text: The condition and characteristic of a vulgar person is that he never looks for either help or harm from himself, but only from externals. The condition and characteristic of a philosopher is that he looks to himself for all help or harm.
significance: Immature people blame circumstances for everything; wise people take responsibility for their own choices and growth.

author: Epictetus
text: The marks of a proficient are that he censures no one, praises no one, blames no one, accuses no one; says nothing concerning himself as being anybody or knowing anything.
significance: Real progress shows in quiet humility: less judging, blaming and accusing others, and less talking up yourself.

author: Epictetus
text: Whatever rules you have adopted, abide by them as laws, and as if you would be impious to transgress them; and do not regard what anyone says of you, for this, after all, is no concern of yours.
significance: Keep the good principles you have chosen as firmly as laws, and do not let gossip or criticism shake you from them.

author: Epictetus
text: Never say of anything, “I have lost it,” but, “I have restored it.”
significance: Everything you have is on loan; when something is taken, see it as returned, which turns bitterness into gratitude.

author: Epictetus
text: Generally then if you would make anything a habit, do it; if you would not make it a habit, do not do it, but accustom yourself to do something else in place of it.
significance: Habits are built by doing and broken by replacing; to change a pattern, practise a better one in its place.

author: Epictetus
text: Know you not that a good man does nothing for the sake of appearance, but for the sake of doing right?
significance: A good person acts rightly because it is right, not to be seen; integrity does not depend on an audience.

author: Epictetus
text: The beginning of philosophy, to him at least who enters on it in the right way and by the door is a consciousness of his own weakness and inability about necessary things
significance: Wisdom begins by honestly admitting how weak and uninformed you are about the things that matter most.

author: Epictetus
text: If then you wish not to be of an angry temper, do not feed the habit: throw nothing on it which will increase it: at first keep quiet, and count the days on which you have not been angry.
significance: Anger grows when fed; starve it by staying quiet when provoked and counting your calm days to build a new habit.

author: Epictetus
text: What a man applies himself to earnestly, that he naturally loves.
significance: We come to love what we give our effort to, so where you invest your attention shapes what you will cherish.

author: Epictetus
text: I have exercised my patience, my abstinence, my co-operation with others; and so we should thank God for what we ought to thank him.
significance: Hardships are chances to practise patience, restraint and cooperation, and that growth is itself something to thank God for.

author: Epictetus
text: The wise and good man neither himself fights with any person, nor does he allow another, so far as he can prevent it.
significance: A good person avoids quarrels and, where possible, makes peace between others rather than stirring conflict.

author: Epictetus
text: Who will not willingly receive a man who is ready to bear a share, as we may say, of the difficulty of his circumstances, and by this very act to ease the burden, by taking a part of it.
significance: People welcome the one who willingly shares their burdens; carrying part of another's load is a mark of true friendship.

author: Epictetus
text: In my opinion no man has had a more profitable difficulty than you have had, if you choose to make use of it as an athlete would deal with a young antagonist.
significance: Treat a hard situation like a training partner: if you choose to use it, it can make you stronger than ease ever would.

author: Epictetus
text: Friends, wait for God: when he shall give the signal and release you from this service, then go to him; but for the present endure to dwell in this place where he has put you.
significance: Stay faithfully at the post where God has placed you, enduring present difficulties until He calls you elsewhere.

author: Epictetus
text: To this matter before all you must attend, that you be never so closely connected with any of your former intimates or friends as to come down to the same acts as he does.
significance: Be careful that friendships, even old ones, never pull you down into habits and actions you know are wrong.

author: Seneca
text: Lay hold of to-day’s task, and you will not need to depend so much upon to-morrow’s. While we are postponing, life speeds by.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Do today's work today; procrastination does not save time, it just lets life slip past while we wait.

author: Seneca
text: Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time. We were entrusted by nature with the ownership of this single thing, so fleeting and slippery that anyone who will can oust us from possession.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Time is the one thing truly ours, yet it slips away easily, often taken by others, so guard how you spend it.

author: Seneca
text: It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Poverty is more about endless wanting than about having little; contentment makes a person rich.

author: Seneca
text: Each day acquire something that will fortify you against poverty, against death, indeed against other misfortunes as well; and after you have run over many thoughts, select one to be thoroughly digested that day.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Take one strengthening idea each day and think it through deeply; small daily lessons build resilience for hard times.

author: Seneca
text: Cleanthes could not have been the express image of Zeno, if he had merely heard his lectures; he shared in his life, saw into his hidden purposes, and watched him to see whether he lived according to his own rules.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Character is passed on by shared life more than by lectures; students learn most from watching whether teachers live what they teach.

author: Seneca
text: Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can. Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual; for men learn while they teach.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Spend time with people who make you better and invest in those you can help; teaching others also teaches you.

author: Seneca
text: To consort with the crowd is harmful; there is no person who does not make some vice attractive to us, or stamp it upon us, or taint us unconsciously therewith.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: The company you keep shapes you; crowds make bad habits seem normal and rub off on us without our noticing.

author: Seneca
text: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Most of what we fear never happens; much of our suffering comes from imagining troubles rather than living them.

author: Seneca
text: No evil is great which is the last evil of all. Death arrives; it would be a thing to dread, if it could remain with you.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Death is the end of evils, not an evil that stays with us; seeing it that way loosens its grip on our fear.

author: Seneca
text: Avoid whatever pleases the throng: avoid the gifts of Chance! Halt before every good which Chance brings to you, in a spirit of doubt and fear; for it is the dumb animals and fish that are deceived by tempting hopes.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Be wary of windfalls and whatever the crowd prizes; easy gifts of fortune can be bait that hooks the unwary.

author: Seneca
text: As for your former prayers, you may dispense the gods from answering them; offer new prayers; pray for a sound mind and for good health, first of soul and then of body.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Change what you pray for: ask first for a sound mind and a healthy soul, and only then for bodily health.

author: Seneca
text: Call boldly upon God; you will not be asking him for that which belongs to another.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Pray boldly for wisdom and goodness; such requests take nothing from anyone else and are always fitting.

author: Seneca
text: Believe me, those who seem to be busied with nothing are busied with the greater tasks; they are dealing at the same time with things mortal and things immortal.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Quiet reflection can look idle but may be the most important work, because it deals with eternal as well as earthly things.

author: Seneca
text: The wise man, I say, self-sufficient though he be, nevertheless desires friends if only for the purpose of practising friendship, in order that his noble qualities may not lie dormant.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Even a self-reliant person needs friends, because friendship is where loyalty, generosity and love are exercised.

author: Seneca
text: The friendship which you portray is a bargain and not a friendship; it regards convenience only, and looks to the results.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: A relationship built only on what you can get from it is a transaction, not friendship; true friends value the person.

author: Seneca
text: We are in the habit of exaggerating, or imagining, or anticipating, sorrow.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: We often make troubles worse by exaggerating them, inventing them or suffering them before they arrive.

author: Seneca
text: Virtue is held too cheap by the man who counts his body too dear.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: If comfort and safety matter most to you, you will trade away integrity too easily when they are threatened.

author: Seneca
text: We should cherish the body with the greatest care; but we should also be prepared, when reason, self-respect, and duty demand the sacrifice, to deliver it even to the flames.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Take good care of your health, but never value it above duty and honour; some things are worth any sacrifice.

author: Seneca
text: The power to inspire fear has caused many men to be in fear.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Leaders who rule by fear end up living in fear themselves; intimidation breeds the very insecurity it imposes.

author: Seneca
text: A soldier’s skill is not at fault if he receives the death-blow through his armour.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Doing everything right does not guarantee the outcome; judge yourself by your effort and conduct, not by results alone.

author: Seneca
text: The mind must be exercised both day and night, for it is nourished by moderate labour; and this form of exercise need not be hampered by cold or hot weather, or even by old age.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Keep your mind active with steady, moderate effort; unlike the body, it can keep growing in any season or age.

author: Seneca
text: In days of peace the soldier performs manœuvres, throws up earthworks with no enemy in sight, and wearies himself by gratuitous toil, in order that he may be equal to unavoidable toil.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Prepare in easy times for hard ones; voluntary discipline now makes you equal to the struggles you cannot avoid later.

author: Seneca
text: We shall be rich with all the more comfort, if we once learn how far poverty is from being a burden.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: If you learn that you could live with little, you can enjoy what you have without anxiety about losing it.

author: Seneca
text: Poverty will keep for you your true and tried friends; you will be rid of the men who were not seeking you for yourself, but for something which you have.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Hard times reveal who your real friends are; those who stay loved you, not what you could give them.

author: Seneca
text: The physician cannot prescribe by letter the proper time for eating or bathing; he must feel the pulse.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Good guidance depends on knowing the person and the moment; general rules must be applied with attention and care.

author: Seneca
text: Much toil remains; to confront it, you must yourself lavish all your waking hours, and all your efforts, if you wish the result to be accomplished.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Real growth takes sustained, wholehearted effort; there is much work left, and it will not be done halfway.

author: Seneca
text: Philosophy bestows this boon upon us; it makes us joyful in the very sight of death, strong and brave no matter in what state the body may be, cheerful and never failing though the body fail us.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Inner wisdom can keep you cheerful and brave even as your body weakens; strength of spirit outlasts physical strength.

author: Seneca
text: Before now men have gone to meet death in a fit of rage; but when death comes to meet him, no one welcomes it cheerfully, except the man who has long since composed himself for death.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Only those who have prepared for death over a lifetime can meet it with peace when it comes.

author: Seneca
text: Follow up the impulse which prompted you to make for all that is best, treading under your feet that which is approved by the crowd.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Keep pursuing what is best, even when it means setting aside what the crowd admires and approves.

author: Seneca
text: An old man learning his A B C is a disgraceful and absurd object; the young man must store up, the old man must use.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Youth is the time to gather wisdom and age the time to use it, so learn the basics early while there is time.

author: Seneca
text: To pay his debt of money, the business man must have a prosperous voyage, the farmer must have fruitful fields and kindly weather; but the debt which your friend owes can be completely paid by mere goodwill.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Debts of friendship are repaid not with money or luck but with sincere goodwill, which anyone can give.

author: Seneca
text: Few words are spoken; but if the mind has truly caught them, they come into their strength and spring up.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: A few good words, truly taken to heart, grow like seeds; teaching does not need many words to bear fruit.

author: Seneca
text: Many of our blessings bring bane to us; for memory recalls the tortures of fear, while foresight anticipates them.
work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (tr. R. M. Gummere)
significance: Memory and foresight are gifts, but they can torment us by reliving past fears and rehearsing future ones.
